utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Ekkehard Withopf and Kimberly Fleming, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. Rodney Dixon and Mr. Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and Mr. Mulalic, legal advisor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The Chamber greets everybody present in the courtroom, the Prosecution, represented by Mr. Withopf; the Defence counsel; the accused; and everybody present in the courtroom. Before we bring in the witness, I would like to clarify certain matters. Firstly, yesterday we mentioned the issue of the duration of testimonies. As you know, in a document that was submitted before the trial, the Prosecution summarised -- provided us with the summaries of the witnesses with the expected timing for every witness; that was between 30 minutes up to 1 or 2 days. This was just an indication of the time that would be required for the witnesses of the Prosecution, and the time indicated was not binding upon the Prosecution. If the Prosecution estimates that they would take more time, they are certainly free to take more time. If the Prosecution says that they will need 45 minutes and they require 1 hour and a half, then they will examine for 1 hour and a half. The only risk that we face is that if the testimony of one witness is not finished within the course of one day, then the witness has to come back on the following day. The same is true of the Defence; the Defence will also have all the time necessary at their disposal for their examination. Having said that, of course I would like to emphasise that if the Prosecution took an hour, then I can't give the Defence two hours for their cross-examination. So when it comes to the timing, we're talking merely about indications of time. The Prosecution obviously will have as much time as necessary to put their questions, and the Defence, when they start calling their witnesses, they will also have as much time as necessary. This is just by way of clarification on this issue. The second issue is to do with cross-examination. As you may well know, you have submitted a motion in order to clarify an oral decision rendered on the 17th of December, 2003. We rendered that decision regarding cross-examination, and I would like to remind you that based on that decision, the issues of context are allowed, but when you ask a question about a context of an event, to the extent possible before you ask the question you have to explain what the purpose of that question is and what are you aiming at with your question. So what are the reasons for you to putting the question, to establish a link between your question and the particular witness. So far things have been going on well, and in the future can you please inform us about the general context of the specific question that you are putting to a particular witness. When it comes to hearsay, hearsay is acceptable on one condition: When you put this type of question, if the witness does provide us with the facts that he heard from somebody else, he has to specify who the origin of the information is. So every time we have to endeavour and identify the source of knowledge. So far we haven't had any problems with that. In the future, if there are any problems, we will deal with them as we go. The third point I wish to raise concerns the rights of the accused and the rights of the Defence to be informed about the admitted exhibits, exhibits admitted into evidence. The accused are not sitting next to their counsel. In the continental law system, the accused sit next to their counsel, and the only way the accused are able to communicate with their counsel is by passing on notes to them. In the future, when we are faced with some important documents produced by the Prosecution, we will have to have one copy for the Chamber, several copies for the Defence counsel, and there will have to be a copy for the accused. Only in that way will the accused be able to follow the exhibits and give their opinions on those exhibits. So far the documents have been provided to the Defence counsel, and they were not provided to the accused. Since we already are making a certain number of copies, I'm sure that the Prosecution will not find it difficult to add to that two more copies for the accused. These were the three points that I wished to raise before we bring in today's witness. Can we please have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I would just like to check whether you can hear me in a language that you can understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you, and I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You were called to testify in this case by the Prosecution. In order to testify, you have to enter a solemn declaration. Before that, I would like to hear your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ivo Fisic. I come from Travnik in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was born on 6 November 1942 in Nevica Polje, Novi Travnik municipality. My father was Marko, and my mother was Andjelka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am an economist, specialising in accountancy for companies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. In 1993, what did you do? What was your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time when these events took place, I was the CEO of a company which was a part of Borac Travnik Cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Can you now, please, read the text of the solemn declaration. Read it in your language, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I shall tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have already told you, first you're going to answer the questions put to you by the representatives of the OTP, on your right-hand side. Try to answer as completely as possible and as precisely as possible. After that, the Defence counsel, sitting on your left, will also ask you some questions. At any point in time, the three Judges, when they deem it is necessary, can also ask you questions. If you have problems understanding a question or any other difficulties with any question, you may ask for the question to be rephrased. If you don't want to answer a question, you have to tell us why you don't want to do that. As you have entered this solemn declaration, you must tell the truth. And if any question is not answered truthfully, you may be liable for false testimony. If any question or any answer you may give may incriminate you, you may refuse to answer. If the Chamber then decides that the witness has to answer the question, the Chamber will inform the witness that there will be no incrimination against him. We are going to start first with the examination-in-chief, and for that purpose I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. Prior to examining the witness, I wish to express my gratitude for the clarifications made today by the Presiding Judge, in particular in respect to the time estimates of the examination-in-chief provided with the Rule 65 ter witness summaries. Examined by Mr. Withopf:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, you informed the Trial Chamber that you were born in Travnik. Can you please also inform the Trial Chamber where you grew up.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I was born in Nevica Polje, 3 and a half kilometres from the town of Travnik and 7 kilometres away from Novi Travnik; however, my village belonged to the municipality of Novi Travnik. In that village, I lived up to 1974, and then I moved to Travnik, to my apartment. And from that moment on, up to the beginning of conflicts, even up to this very day I have lived at that same address.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber whether you joined the JNA. And if so, can you please provide us with the dates when you joined it and when you left it.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I served in the JNA from the 18th of September, 1963, to the end of February 1965. I served in Umag in Istria. This was my compulsory military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Fisic, did you have a military rank once you left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. When I left the JNA, I became a corporal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a university degree?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have an associate degree. I graduated in Sarajevo. I graduated as a part-time student of the university in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already informed the Trial Chamber that in 1992 and 1993 you were living and working in Travnik. What actually was your work about during this time?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I was the general manager of a work organisation which was a part of the Borac company, which was basically a publishing house that also engaged in the trade of printed matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having lived and worked in Travnik in 1992 and early 1993, did there come a time when you noticed foreigners in this area of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in the course of 1992 foreign citizens started arriving in Travnik. Their general appearance was different. One could conclude that they were Arabs, I don't know where from, but it was obvious that they were Arabs. They wore very distinctive uniforms that I noticed when they came for prayers to the mosques. Some of them also wore military uniforms, camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ones who wore military camouflage uniforms, did you see them carrying any weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Some of them - not many - wore -- carried long-barrelled rifles. They had their headquarters in a building where I had used to work, which belonged to the General Trading Company. That's where they had their headquarters or the command or something like that. There was a flag on that building, very visible. I had never seen such a flag before in Travnik. It was a flag -- a black flag with Arabic inscription in golden thread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These headquarters of the foreign citizens you are referring to, just for clarification, in which town was it located?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: In Travnik, in Marsal Tito Street, in a building where I used to work which belonged to the General Trading Company. Before my company bought this building, it housed the Vlasic Hotel. It was in the very centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point in time, 1992 and early 1993, did your community use a certain word to describe these Arab-looking foreigners?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the very beginning, they were referred to as Mujahedins. I never heard the word before. I didn't know what this meant. However, people referred to them and recognised them as Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge whether such Mujahedins at this point in time or later on got granted Bosnian citizenship?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know something about that. Between 1981 and 1994, I discharged the duties of the president of the executive board, that is, the government of the Municipal Assembly of Travnik. From the officials of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, I learnt that these foreign citizens were being awarded citizenship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For clarification, the citizenship they have been awarded, was it the Bosnian-Herzegovinian citizenship?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Most probably. Most probably. In 1992, I don't remember exactly whether at that moment Bosnia and Herzegovina was an internationally recognised state. However, they were given certificates from the secretariat, based on which they could obtain citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a remark. On page 8, lines 10 to 11, when the witness was talking about this black flag that he saw on the building of the trading company, he said one sentence which was not translated. So could we please have the witness confirm that he indeed said that so that it may be recorded subsequently or may he be asked the question again. The witness said, "I never saw such a flag amongst Bosnian Muslims." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is what I said. And I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This hasn't been recorded, so I wanted it to be -- to enter the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having said that, the witness confirms that he had never seen this flag before among the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among Bosnian Muslims. Very well, then. Mr. Withopf, since we heard this clarification, can you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, did there come a time when you got involved with the HVO either on a military basis or on a civilian basis?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: The presidency of the Municipality of Travnik, I think it was from the 20th to the 23rd of July 1992, it had eight conclusions according to which certain reconstructions of the executive power in Travnik should be implemented. The objective was to try to solve the tension, the animosity that was manifest in that area. According to some considerations, they thought that I and others were people who can contribute to calming the situation down. They suggested that I and some other people within the HVO, the so-called HVO government, attempt to adopt positions that would be closer to those of the representatives of the Muslim authorities, and the intention was that the power structure should be a single structure at one point in time. But this was all to no avail. And now I'm referring to the military and police units and so-called paramilitary formations, paramilitary units. We didn't manage to get them over to our side, and as a result, that government had no success up until the time when the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, during the time you worked for the HVO as a civilian, did you wear at any point in time a military uniform? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: No. Government representatives didn't wear uniforms. We wanted the usual civilian clothes. And none of the representatives of that government ever wore a uniform of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber the situation or the relationship between the Croats and the Muslims in early 1993 in the region of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: From that critical moment, when it was concluded that something should be done in order to reduce the tension and the animosity and the lack of trust, as far as I understood the situation, it was increasingly complex from day to day. We attempted to unify certain services, such as the post office, the food supply for units and for the population. However, at that time, there were some invisible forces at work which I didn't recognise immediately, and they disrupted all these attempts. And wishes of the population to form some sort of a single body, a single authority, was fruitless. We didn't wear uniforms, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did the Mujahedin play, if any, in creating the tension and the animosity between the two ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I believe that the role they played was very important, because this lack of trust was increasingly evident. There were conflicts between them and units which were in the village of Ovcarevo or in Miskica Brdo, in those passes to the lines in Bila Buce [phoen] Conflicts could break out in those areas. So these people were not authorities who instilled trust but they instilled fear in others. At the time, you could hear people crying "Allah-U-Ekber" and "Tekbir," other such cries that made the population afraid. But you could see that there were some citizens with those people who used to be hooligans when they were minors or they had already been convicted and so on. The citizens of Travnik and of the municipality noticed this, and naturally this made the people afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Fisic, when these tensions and animosities resulted in an actual conflict?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the town itself, within its urban limits, this did not occur. But in the south-west part, in the Kalibunar settlement, such incidents did occur, and as a rule, at night there were skirmishes between the police, the HVO, who were stationed up there between regular and irregular units. But at night it was a problem for the population of that area in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber more concrete -- more concretely the situation in June 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: In June 1993, they started setting up a lot of checkpoints. Whoever was -- dominated would set up the checkpoint. They checked each other. It was unnecessary. It was more difficult to pass through. I'm talking about the year 1993. So in Travnik, in May I think it was, some Croats were arrested and taken away, some Croats who had been found in the street. They were taken to Stari Grad, the old town. I found out that they'd been arrested because information had arrived that in the south-eastern part of Travnik, Kalibunar, an incident had occurred and one or several Muslim members of some units had been captured. So at that time, the reaction was to arrest some Croatian citizens of Travnik, take them to the Stari Grad area, which is where they stayed for a while. They were then transferred to Plava Voda. That is a source where there is a restaurant. It's in the immediate vicinity of the Medresa, and they stayed there for a certain while. And after some politicians from the Muslim side intervened, they were released. They were allowed to go home. In fact, nothing else happened to them, apart from the fact that they were arrested, taken to Stari Grad, then transferred to Plava Voda, which is where they spent the day. They stayed there until sometime at night. But they were returned to their homes without having been maltreated. That's one of the details that points to the fact that this lack of trust was on the rise. I attended a meeting, a circle of combatants from Travnik. They were military commanders, the president of the presidency of the Travnik Municipality, and the president of the HVO. And at that meeting, they discussed how to deal with the situation, how to solve the problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, can I interrupt you at this point. You were mentioning that in June 1993 they started setting up a lot of checkpoints. Whom are you actually referring to in saying "they set up a lot of checkpoints"?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to all those who at that time were in a position to carry weapons and wear uniforms, members of all units, of military units, of paramilitary, police units, all those who at that time carried weapons and wore uniforms. All those who had power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In June 1993, Mr. Fisic, who were the military commanders of the ABiH in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: The late Colonel Alagic, Mr. Fikret Cuskic, Sipic - I don't know his first name, Ahmed Mesanovic, Enes Balagija, Osman Poric. Those are the people I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please go in a bit more respect to the military units they have commanded at the time, as far as you can tell.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I recognised them as Territorial Defence units. These were Krajina units of some kind. I don't know how they were organised exactly. And there were some so-called HOS, Croatian armed forces, units. And this is what I know about those units in Travnik and its surroundings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on, Mr. Fisic, to October 1993. Did there come a time when you have been arrested in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: With your permission, there was something else I would like to add about the animosity and other important events that occurred in Travnik, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead, but keep it brief.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, at that time the commander of the Travnik HVO, Ivica Stojak, was killed at the exit from Travnik to the east. He was killed by units who were present in the area at the time. These were army units. Secondly, Dana Gaso was killed in her flat by some militant units; that's what they say. There were two victims in Travnik, and this was a reason for even more animosity and an even greater lack of understanding. Yes. On the 18th of October, I was arrested in my flat in a very rough manner. When I was arrested, they didn't just arrest me but they also stole property from my flat. They maltreated my wife and the neighbours who were in my home at the time. One of the Croatian neighbours was arrested together with me, whereas the other neighbour, Mr. Kulovac and his wife, were maltreated for a long time because they were in my flat, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, can you please go in more detail. Who arrested you and your Croatian neighbour and who is actually your Croatian neighbour? Can you please give us the name.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: At that critical point in time, about an hour and a half before I was officially arrested, I went from my sister's flat - her name is Marija Martinovic - which is in Zvijezda I, the Zvijezda building. That's about 3 or 4 hundred metres from my flat. So I was leaving her flat, and it was about 6.00 or 6.30 p.m. As I was going along the road to my flat, a vehicle stopped in front of me and the people in the vehicle asked me to help them and to tell them where Mr. Salko Beba's flat was. I noticed that a local man was in the vehicle; at least, that's what he looked like. And there was an Arab. I wasn't able to answer their question because I didn't know where Salko Beba lived. But I told them to ask a group of citizens who were in the vicinity, three or four of them, and I told them they should ask them as to the whereabouts of Salko Beba's flat. I then continued to my flat. When I got to my flat, I had to go to the toilet, which I did. I then decided to remain in the bathroom, to have a shower, and so on. While I was getting ready to have a shower, my wife called me and said that someone had appeared at the door and wanted to come into the flat. She said that the person said he was a friend of mine, but he didn't want to introduce himself, and naturally my wife didn't allow him to enter the flat. I then abandoned the idea of having a shower. We called the local police. Part of the local police force is in the building in which I live. It's called Amerikanka. That's the name of the building. And the police arrived immediately. They listened to what my wife had to say about the person who appeared. They made a record of what she said. They had a look around the hall of the building. They didn't notice anything, but they said if this happened again that we should call them immediately. My neighbour Kulovac came to my flat immediately. He heard something was happening. He wanted to see what was going on and to see if he could help me or perhaps he just wanted to talk to me. His wife also stayed on in my flat. After them, Kazimir Pobric also appeared. He also lives in that building but a few floors further up. But he worked for the Territorial Defence staff of Travnik municipality. He was returning from his duties, and he thought that his wife was with us. So he appeared in my flat too. Afterwards, some people appeared again. They wanted to enter the flat. In a similar manner, as on the previous occasion, we didn't open the door. They didn't introduce themselves, and they went away. Maybe half an hour later, perhaps more, perhaps less, someone knocked on the door again. But after the second time someone appeared, we informed the police. The police came. They introduced themselves as the police. We opened the door, but in fact the people who arrested me entered. The first person to enter was someone with a sabre. This person was wearing a Palestinian-style head scarf. He was followed by a number of members of some kind of units. I then hid behind a piece of furniture to avoid being within the reach of that sabre. Some of those members entered after this person, and as there was no electricity in the town at the time, in part of the flat there was a candle burning and in front of that candle there was a man who was standing there. He had my phone book in his hands. It had been taken from me when I was attacked on one occasion. This was done by the Muslim forces located in the Stari Grad. I saw him holding that phone book, and I think that person was a civilian. I couldn't see him very well, but I did recognise this phone book that had been taken from me. He ordered me to put my shoes on, to get dressed. He said that I was under arrest. And I was a bit confused. And that's how they took me out of my flat. I live on the second floor. Then there were two soldiers at the exits from the floors on the building. I could see that they were soldiers in camouflage uniforms and they had weapons on them; that is to say, they were carrying rifles. They took me to some sort of all-terrain vehicle. I think it was a Niva all-terrain vehicle. They put me into the vehicle. At the back they put a hood over my head -- they put a cap over my head and they told me to lie down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, may I please stop you there. I have two questions for clarification: You said that the person with the sabre was accompanied by soldiers. Do you know by soldiers of which army?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: This group was called the MOS, Muslim armed forces. I think that's what it means. And they were billeted in Stari Grad in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second question: The two soldiers who were waiting outside, which armed forces did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I think they belonged to the same forces. I think it was the same unit. They were from some MOS unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, a third question for clarification: Have you been the only one who has been arrested, or has there been another person been arrested at the very same occasion?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: On that same occasion, Pobric Kazimir was taken out of my flat and taken to the same vehicle and the same hood was put over his head. He was issued the same orders as I had been issued, and then he was driven away in an unknown direction. The drive lasted for quite a long time. And when the vehicle stopped, they got us out of the vehicle. It was already night-time. But they had some sort of torches. I could see that we were entering someone's house. There was a metal fence. The house was 20, 30, or 50 paces from the place where they got us out of the car. And then we were taken into the house. But at the time, I wasn't sure of where we were, but I was sure that we were quite far from Travnik because we had travelled for quite a long time. As they were taking us in the house -- when they took us in the house, they put us in a room. When I entered the room, I noticed that there were some other people inside. I immediately recognised Dragan Popovic, Professor Ivo Rajkovic, and there was a third person whom I didn't know at the time. This person was a minor. His name was Dalibor Adzaip. When we were lined up in that room, Popovic, Kazimir, and myself entered the room. Then the beatings -- then the beating started, and I think that Popovic was the one who fared the worst. And I noticed that the person who was dealing the blows was well trained in karate. And this person was an Arab, whereas there were a group of soldiers and they would kick some of us or punch others. It depended. Then the beating stopped. We were told to take our watches off, our rings off, our shoes off, the jacket that I had on me. So they took those away and left us standing there in our shirts and socks. They then tied us up with some sort of rope and they brought us a blanket on which we sat down. Then this Arab appeared again. He gave us all nicknames of some kind, on the basis of the way we looked. We were all pigs. Some was a big pig, some was a small pig, some was a Serbian pig, some were thin pigs. Those are the sort of nicknames we were given. And then the beating continued. And if you weren't able to say whether you were a big pig or a small pig, you -- you would get the beating. If you realised that you were a big pig or a small pig, then the beating would stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, may I just stop you there for a number of questions for clarification. The three individuals which were detained in the same building as you have been detained - namely, the ones you mentioned, Dragan Popovic, Professor Ivan Rajkovic, and Dalibor Adzaip - what was or what is or what has been their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I am Croat; Rajkovic is a Croat; Popovic was from a mixed marriage; and Dalibor Adzaip as well was also from a mixed marriage. His father is a Serb and his mother is a Croat. So I don't know what the latter two declared themselves as. Actually, Dragan Popovic was also from a mixed marriage. His father is a Serb and his mother --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear what the mother was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please, Mr. Fisic, repeat what ethnicity the mother of Mr. Dragan Popovic has been.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: She was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Fisic, the profession of Mr. Dragan Popovic at the time you were arrested together with him?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Dragan Popovic is an economist. At that moment, he was the financial director of Sebesic forestry company. Before that, he was a member of the reserve police, according to the then-formation of the police structures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you and the persons you just mentioned who were detained together with you, where did they actually live prior to being arrested?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: We all lived in the town of Travnik in urban locations, Zvijezda I, Amerikanka. And the distance -- the diameter of that area of that is about 400 metres. We knew each other well during the war and before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, you were mentioning an Arab and you were mentioning soldiers being around and actually inflicting the beatings. Do you recall which army these soldiers belonged to?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: At that moment, I didn't know. I later on learned that it was the camp of El Mujahed forces. In that camp, there were some foreign citizens, but there also were local lads. And this was all a military unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were describing the beatings, Mr. Fisic, which were inflicted on you. Can you please continue and go in more detail.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: As they entered the room where we were, this beating lasted up to midnight, and the beatings were random. Some were hit in the head; some were hit in the back. Dragan Popovic was as a rule beaten by the Arab, and this was done professionally, I would say. Sometime after midnight the beating in our room stopped, but from the next-door room we heard noise and wailings, and I recognised the voice of Zvonko Kukric, my ex-associate, who was arrested with the priest Vinko from Travnik. This was before we were arrested. So the priest from Travnik was arrested together with officials of Caritas, Zvonko Kukric and Petric's brother. A few nuns were also arrested on that occasion. From the moment they started bursting into our room and stopped, they moved to this other room. And really, it was painful to hear the continuation of the torture that was happening there and the sound of the wailing that reached our room. And that's how that night, between the 18th and the 19th of October, 1993, went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly, Mr. Fisic, that all prisoners who were detained together with you were beaten to the more or less same extent?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Popovic was really much more heavily beaten than the rest of us. Popovic suffered most and was exposed most to the torture and heavy Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The beatings inflicted on you, did they result in any injury?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. On the following day, Wednesday, the 19th October, sometime in the course of the day we were moved from that room and we were joined -- the priest who had -- who was already not there. I noticed blood on the walls and the window that was in that room was completely blocked with black curtains, so we were moved from the first room to the second room. But Priest Vinko or any others were no longer there. We stayed there until late in the night. And then on that second night they also would enter the room and they would beat us, but less than the first day. That's how we fared on Wednesday and on the night. And then on the early -- in the early morning hours of Thursday, the door opened, and this Arab motioned to me with a finger to come out, and he motioned to the others as well. We were tied with ropes in that corridor, the corridor of that house. And that's how they escorted us. And we started moving forward. As we were leaving this house, I saw a sticker on the door, a sticker such as put in Catholic houses showing that they were blessed on the 6th of January. So I was wondering where I was but I couldn't guess. We were taken out of the house, and we were taken across the village road to a meadow. And as we were walking across this meadow, there were uniformed soldiers lined in a semicircle. The four of us were walking. Professor Rajkovic was not with us. There were just three of us, Popovic, Fisic, and Adzaip, and Kazimir Pobric. There were actually four of us. So these soldiers were lined in a semicircle. And as we were passing across this meadow they were shouting, "Tekbir, Allah-U-Ekber," and some other things, but I could not understand those other things. We had been ill-treated. I can't give you all the details. We were brought to the end of this semicircle, and I noticed that a graveyard had been dug for maybe two or three people, two at the most. An Arab was standing there, an Arab in a uniform, and he was the one who was conducting this ritual of shouting which went on continuously in a high-pitched voice. They were shouting. My hands were untied. Popovic was the last in -- as they untied me, they gave the rope to somebody in the semicircle, and at that moment on one road that was there an all-terrain vehicle arrived that I had seen in Travnik already. Its windows were dark. It stopped at an elevation from which the passengers could watch what was going on below that elevation. The vehicle came. We were all untied. At that moment, Popovic was taken forward in a very coarse way and he was thrown on the ground. Then some soldiers jumped on him, and the Arab called Hasan to step out. Hasan stepped out. Somebody handed him a knife, and that's how he started slaughtering Popovic, who was lying underneath the soldier. I was not all there, but I could see that Hasan was doing a very bad job slaughtering him. And another soldier approached the body, a very sturdy and heavily-built man, and he completed the slaughtering in a very brutal way. It's very hard for me to describe how this was done. When the head was separated from the body, the Arab brought the head to me and forced me to kiss that head from the dead body. And that's what happened. And then the body and the head were taken to the grave, and the knife was placed by the body but in a wrong way, against the ritual. So the soldier had to approach the body again to change the position of the knife. And then we were ordered to fill the grave with our hands and legs and all the while the shouting went on. And the Lasva Valley was shaking from the -- from the strength of these sounds and the shouting. Then the soldiers approached me. They twisted my arm behind my back and took me back to the house where we were before. As I was returning, down a slope I noticed a school in Guca Gora, and I also saw the sandpit Pese across two hills. So my assumption was that I was somewhere in the area of Mehurici, in the north of Travnik municipality. I didn't know what the name of the village was. I subsequently learned that I was in Bobasi hamlet in Orahovac village. I subsequently learned that when I went to show the investigators where the body of Popovic had been buried. That's when I learned that the area is called Orahovac and that the hamlet where the execution took place was Bobasi and Pese and it all belonged to the local commune of Mehurici. I was familiar with Mehurici, but I was not familiar with these hamlets. So I was returned. And as I was being returned, the soldier kept on telling me, "It is your turn tomorrow. That's what we have planned for you." We were again put in the same room from which we had been taken. Kazimir Pobric was given the task to tell in very great detail what the ritual was like. Whenever he omitted an important detail, he would be beaten and he would have to start from the very beginning. He was telling the story to Rajkovic, who was absent from this act of execution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just stop you there for a moment, Mr. Fisic. Do you recall, Mr. Fisic, how many soldiers were present when this ritual beheading of Mr. Dragan Popovic took place?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I believe at least 50 members of that unit were there, maybe even more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, you described to some extent the area where all this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: With the permission of the Trial Chamber, I will now show the witness a photograph. We will use the Sanction technology. We have also the necessary photocopies available in hard copy. Can, please, one copy be made available to the witness, please. For the information of the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel, this photograph has been taken by the Dutch forensic photographers in the course of the year 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Do you have a felt-tip pen or something? I would like to make some markings on the photo. I would like to mark some of these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be provided with such a pen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you make the markings -- before you make the markings, Mr. Fisic, can you please first inform us what you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I can see the area where we stayed and which I saw when I came to help the investigators and tell them where Mr. Popovic had been buried. That is when I had the occasion to inspect the area more thoroughly, much more than in those moments when I was being taken to and from that execution. I recognised the building where we were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, does this photograph show the area where the beheading of Mr. Dragan Popovic took place?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I cannot be absolutely sure, but I believe that this was the route that we took. And here, where you see the ruins of a building, this is the area where the vehicle was and this is where the execution took place. The distance is about 3 to 4 hundred metres. This is Pese hamlet. This is Bobasi hamlet. I also notice this big building. Later on, I learnt that this was the Mujahedin camp. It belonged to a shepherd who was tending to his sheep while I was there. And this is all that I can see in this photo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, you made a number of markings. Can you please mark the different buildings and the killing site with numbers from 1 to 4 or 5.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Number 1 is the building where we were placed; number 2 is a family house in front of which the execution took place; number 3 is the part of the road where the vehicle was and from which people were observing the execution; and number 4 is the Mujahedin camp in the building that belonged to a shepherd who was tending to his sheep in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the ease of reference, can you please at the very bottom of the photograph write down what the different numbers actually mean.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, since my knowledge of the Croatian language is a limited one, can you please tell us what you have written down.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Number 4, "The Mujahedin camp." "The building of the Mujahedin camp, a newly built building, which did not exist before the conflict. It was built during the conflict --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic -- Mr. Fisic, this is just for clarification. Can you please just repeat what you have written down. This is for the ease of reference. Don't give any further explanation. Just read out what you have written down.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Number 1, "The house where we were." Number 2, "The house in front of which the execution took place." Number 3, "The position of the vehicle." Number 4, "The Mujahedin camp."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Fisic. This area which you can see on the photograph, is it also known as the area of Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: No, not really. Guca Gora is something else. It's a separate area. But they are very close. This is the area of Mehurici. Guca Gora is in a different area, not very far but different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, can you please sign and date the photograph you just made the markings on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, today is the 30th of January.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you give me an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution wishes to tender this photograph into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we then have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P52.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. With the permission of the Presiding Judge, I would like to continue for one or two further minutes before the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were mentioning, Mr. Fisic, the beatings that were inflicted on all of you during your detention in the area you just identified on the photograph. What was the result of such beatings in respect to you? Did you have any injuries, any serious injuries?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I can tell you how I felt. We did not have any medical assistance. I was beaten most in the head. I would like to take the opportunity to see whether somebody could examine me here, because I still have problems. My head was banged on the wall, my ribs were broken, and I had contusions all over the body. I was black and blue all over. What degree of invalidity would that be, I don't know. I did not have anybody to complain to. Nobody ever asked us until the following Thursday how we were. On the 4th of October, I had first contacts with people who asked me something officially. In the meantime, almost every night an Arab would enter our room to talk to us, to try and persuade us of things. They didn't beat us; they just talked to us. And then on that Thursday --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic -- Mr. Fisic, could I please stop you there. The very last question before the break: You were informing the Trial Chamber that your ribs were broken. What about your nose?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: That was the result of the beating on the first night. My shirt was all covered in blood and my bone in the nose must have been broken. I'm generally healthy, so I could sustain the beatings better than others, maybe. My shirt was stained with blood, and this all lasted until the 4th of October. We couldn't bathe. We couldn't wash our faces. The hygienic conditions were non-existent, so to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Fisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That's it for the time being. And I would suggest to make the break before I continue with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A 25-minute break. We shall resume at five minutes to 11.00. Witness, the usher is going to take you to a room where you will be able to rest. We shall resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume with the examination-in-chief. Mr. Withopf, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, prior to the break, you were informing the Trial Chamber that you couldn't wash your faces and the hygienic conditions Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were non-existent. And you were informing the Trial Chamber that a bone in your nose must have been broken. The beatings, did they result at some point in time that you actually lost consciousness?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: On the 20th, in the afternoon, when they took me out of that room into the hall, Hasan and the slaughterer, the person who had executed the other man, approached me and they forced me to identify the person who had committed the execution. I really did know who the person was. I identified the person, but I decided not to admit it. I thought that would be better for me. As I didn't say that I recognised the person who had committed the act, they beat me. Hasan was a slightly-built person. His blows weren't that severe, weren't that threatening. But on -- at one point in time this slaughterer said, "Now this Ustasha will see how I can beat," and after the second or third blow I fell down in the hall. And when I came to, I was in the room in which the other detainees were present. I don't know how long I remained lying on the floor or how long it took for me to regain consciousness. These are things that I still don't know to this very day. So this was the most severe beating that I received on that Thursday in the afternoon. In the evening hours, I wasn't maltreated -- not severely maltreated. But on the contrary, one of the local men - I think his name was Muradif, and I think he comes from Kakanj or Moscanica, that's what he told me - he must have taken pity on me. He gave me half a litre of milk and a pear and said I should take care to hide it very well. So he helped me a lot when he gave me these things. It was humane. And that was between Thursday and Friday. On Friday -- the date was the 21st -- Friday wasn't too bad, as far as the beatings are concerned. We were given meals and some sort of dishes. I don't know how much we needed or didn't need, but we were provided with these meals. And in the early evening someone from our cell was taken to be questioned. It was Professor Rajkovic. This question lasted for a while. And when he returned, he said that someone had appeared from Travnik. He hadn't recognised him, he didn't know who he was, and he didn't tell us who he was. In the meantime, I was called to talk to someone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I please stop you there for a moment. You informed the Trial Chamber about ribs being broken, about the nose -- the bone in the nose broken. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber whether anything happened to your hands.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was on that Friday. One of the guards, he was particularly bad. He said that he came from the area of Maglaj, somewhere around there, and he said that he had been expelled by the Croats and he said he wasn't doing us any more harm an the harm the Croats did to him. At one point he gave he a truncheon to hit him, Rajkovic, with, but I noticed that this was of some -- it was made of some sort of heated metal. I grasped it and I burnt my hand. But later on he didn't insist on me picking it up from the floor. It was a practical joke. It was a minor detail. So that was the kind of act that he had committed. But that guard was very brutal to everyone. So that is what happened to my hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, did there come a time when you were transferred to somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I have to say that the conversation on Friday was one that I wasn't capable of conducting, engaging in. I wasn't very concentrated. But I remember that the person questioning me, a local man whom I did not recognise, he asked me who the other prominent Croats in Travnik were and he particularly asked me about Mrs. Saric and her whereabouts. She is a teacher. I couldn't answer the question, and he asked me, "Who are the other prominent Croats?" What is important for me is that Kazimir Pobric went for such a discussion, for such a questioning. And after that questioning, he was no longer in the camp with us. I was told that he returned to Travnik, and in fact he was returned to Travnik on that Friday. So that's the 20th, on Friday. On Saturday -- Saturday was a fairly normal day. And from Saturday onwards, we weren't maltreated until our return to Travnik. No maltreatment such as the maltreatment we had received up until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I please stop you there. During the time you had been detained and maltreated, did anybody on your behalf make any attempt to inform anybody in power about your abduction?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Please don't insist on me telling you the name of this person, a friend of mine who held an important position -- an important professional position in Zenica at the time. He found a way of finding out where we were and he informed my wife of the fact that on that Thursday I hadn't been eliminated. Please don't insist on me telling you his name. It wouldn't be fair. He found a way of gaining access to the Mujahedin, to the camp, and of checking to see whether we were alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your wife or anybody else approach anybody with the aim to get you released?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of the doctors from Travnik who like my friend from Zenica had a way of getting information, he came one evening, perhaps on Friday or Saturday, and he informed my wife that I was alive and hadn't been executed. So that's the second person from Travnik, this doctor, who gave such good news to my wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your wife make any attempt to get you released?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes. My wife and sister, they were in Travnik in their flats. They undertook everything they could. They contacted international organisations in Travnik and the state authorities, the president of the municipality, the police and the military commander, the deceased Mr. Alagic and Mr. Cuskic. They contacted them and tried to get them to help. And I must say that the military authorities, with Mr. Alagic and Mr. Cuskic at their head, did everything they could to help my wife. And I know that many of the citizens of Travnik asked for our situation to be clarified -- my situation, Rajkovic's, and Adzaip's situation. So there was cooperation among these forces. Alagic and Cuskic undertook certain actions and they informed my wife as to what they were doing in order to obtain our release from that camp. I should point out that that lasted from the 20th to the 4th, this attempt to get us released and the pressure that was exerted in order to obtain our release from that camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic -- Mr. Fisic, did your wife and your sister inform Mr. Alagic and the military authorities about the location of the camp you were detained?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes. They believed we were in the area of Mehurici. They claimed that we were there all the time, and they said we could be found in those hamlets. And my wife obtained information according to which Mr. Alagic and Mr. Cuskic could do this, because they had released one of their members who had fallen foul of the Mujahedin. So if he could do so, he could -- they could also get us released. They had influence of some kind. The information that my wife obtained surprised Alagic and Cuskic. They wondered how she knew about that. They insisted on this being said. But my wife didn't reveal her sources, didn't tell them where she had obtained this information. But she asked them to tell her whether this was true or not. She said if it wasn't true, she would withdraw her request; but if it was true, they should take the same steps to get us released. And they really did take certain steps to obtain our release. On the 4th of April, I was taken out of my room. I was taken into another room, where I was questioned. The position -- the people were positioned in the room in the same way as the people are positioned in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to your transfer. You were telling us that on Saturday, the 6th of November, 1993, you were transferred back to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 6th of November, 1993. I must tell you that that's my birthday. I was taken to Travnik much to everyone's surprise, because the process of transferring us from Orasac to Travnik lasted from the 4th to the 5th, which is when the late Mr. Alagic informed my wife, in the evening of the 5th at about 1800 hours, that there was no hope for our release and that there was nothing more he could do to obtain our release. He said, "I can do no more in order to save your husband and the others who are up there now." On Saturday, the 6th of November, at about half past 12.00, we were taken to Travnik to the barracks. At the time of Austro-Hungarian, it was also a barracks. I'd been blindfolded there in an all-terrain vehicle. I was taken down into a basement where there was a prison for BH Army members who were in prison on account of certain actions, and there was also a group of, I think, about ten HVO members who had fallen into the hands of the army members in various ways, and that's where these people were being detained. So on the 6th of November, at about half past 12.00, I was taken there in an all-terrain vehicle. And when they untied my hands and took the blindfold off, they took me into another room where I saw Professor Rajkovic crying and a BH Army member whom I didn't know. He was sitting on a chair and explaining something to Professor Rajkovic concerning our arrest. When I entered that room, that member addressed me by my name. He said, "It's no longer necessary for you to be afraid. You're in good hands now. Nothing more will happen to you." But I was suspicious. I asked him, "Who are you? Who can promise such things to me?" He said, "I'm Salko Beba." I had heard of Salko Beba, but I didn't know him personally. I then asked him if that was the case. "If everything is fine now, is there some way for us to inform my family. My wife and my sister, can we inform them that I'm here. Tell them that I'm in the barracks." He did this. But I must point out that before he did so, Alagic had already informed my family that I arrived and he congratulated my wife because it was my birthday. So that's as far as my arrival day is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Fisic, you are making reference to the barracks in Travnik. For clarification, are these the former JNA barracks in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the former JNA barracks. It's a compound which is called a barracks. It contains various buildings, various facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You were mentioning a certain individual named Salko Beba, whom you met during your detention in the JNA -- former JNA barracks in Travnik. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what the position of Mr. Salko Beba has been at the time you talked to him.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can say for sure that at the time he had the position of an assistant for Mr. Alagic, a security assistance. I found out about this two or three days later, because I went to give him a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the statement you went to give him about?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salko Beba called me into my office [as interpreted], which is on the grounds of the barracks. He was interested in everything that -- he was interested in everything that had happened to us from the time we were arrested and he wanted to know what the conditions were like up there, et cetera. I think that my statement was a little more detailed than the statement I am giving you here today. And I gave the statement to Mr. Salko Beba. He listened to me. He listened to what I had to say up until the time of the execution. There was a recording clerk who made a note of everything. He then jumped up. He was excited. He left the room and left me and the secretary there and he didn't come back to hear the end of my statement. But one of -- someone else who worked with him - his name is Jasmin - continued to take the statement. And I gave the statement in a manner which is similar to the manner in which I'm giving a statement here today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, were you able to inform Mr. Salko Beba, the security officer to Mr. Alagic, about the fact and the circumstances Mr. Popovic has been beheaded?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, in detail. I told him about this in great detail. That is the last thing he questioned me about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also inform other individuals about what you had experienced in the detention facility in the area of Orasac?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: When we asked to be seen by Mr. Fikret Cuskic so that he could explain to us the reason for which we were there, because we were among a group of Croatian detainees, of HVO members, Mr. Cuskic received us in a very gentlemanly and courteous manner and he said that as far as we were concerned, he had no business with us as a soldier. He'd been ordered to see us. And as there was no room, he said that in a few days' time, five days at the most, we would no longer be kept with the HVO members who had fallen into the hands of BH army members in various ways. On that occasion, we told Mr. Cuskic about everything, not in such detail but we gave him a brief outline about what had happened. He was very nervous when listening to all we had to say, and I think he would have preferred it if we hadn't informed him about this. But we did. And he said, "There are some units I can't deal with in this area. I have to solve this issue. We'll call President Izetbegovic." And this is what happened. Mr. Izetbegovic came to Travnik while we were still in the basement of that prison, in that building where the prison was located. And the next thing that Mr. Cuskic did: Rajkovic was a sick man, but in two days' time in the clinic which was also on the compound, I left two days after Rajkovic and I think he gave us more than he could have given us. He gave us a room next to where patients were kept. And we were under medical surveillance from that time onwards. I have asked for a general checkup and that was done. They determined that there had been some serious injuries. I didn't receive the medical documentation, which probably remained in the archives of the Travnik General Hospital. On the grounds of that barracks, the name of the doctor was Begzad. He was from Kljuc, and he treated us very correctly. When we arrived there, I don't think we had any more problems. On the contrary, the conditions there were very good, given their possibilities at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, at the time you arrived in the Travnik barracks and had your meeting with Mr. Salko Beba, were your injuries still visible?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, the injuries were visible. They were very -- we looked very ugly because we were unshaven, we hadn't had a bath for a long time. We looked terrible. You could see the bruises. You could see the injuries on our bodies. But we were alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned several times, Mr. Fisic, the name of Mr. Fikret Cuskic. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber who Mr. Fikret Cuskic is and what his position has been at the time.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I met him when he was the commander of some 27th Krajina unit. I don't know which one exactly. He held the rank of a major. He was an officer par excellence. That's what he looked like, too. I'm just speaking about what concerns Ivo Fisic, Rajkovic, and the others who were detained there. He was very fair towards us. He knew what the rules of conduct were, and he was very knowledgeable about military matters. And he didn't treat us in a bad manner. I don't know whether he treated others badly, but in our case he was fair. He took all the steps he could to make it better for us and to prevent us from being BH army detainees. He tried to avoid this. And when my family, the Pobric family, and the Adzaip family gave some sort of military agreement for us to leave, he wrote something down. He said he was allowing the evacuation of families from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, other than providing Mr. Salko Beba and Mr. Fikret Cuskic with details about your experiences in the Orasac camp, did you inform any members of international organisations about the experiences you made?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Everyone knew that we'd been detained two hours after our arrest. So some groups that had a positive attitude towards me - I have such a document - they informed me and my wife and sister were in favour of this information being provided -- well, they were aware of this, but no one came when we were in Orasac. When I got to the barracks in Travnik, the first person to appear was the representative of the international monitors, followed by Mrs. Mary Jo, who was the regional head of the Red Cross whose headquarters were in Zenica. We told these representatives about everything that I have said here but in greater detail, so they had firsthand knowledge about these events. Mr. Cuskic made this possible, and there was no fear that we might be maltreated because of this. So they were informed. They were aware of the case, and Mrs. Mary Jo took charge of the entire case and she took steps to get us released from our detention in the barracks. From the management of the barracks, we received their agreement that whenever we wanted to go to town we could do that, on a daily basis. But we had to inform them of this -- we could go to town but under -- under escort. We had to be escorted by guards, by armed soldiers. But at the time when I went to the town, I heard that there were a number of accusations that concerned me. They would say that I'd done -- committed certain crimes, and this is what I heard when I would go to town with the soldiers who were escorting us. So we had a limited form of freedom, and this continued up until the time when we asked what was going to happen to us. We wanted to know why we were there. If we were guilty, we wanted an indictment issued to say that we were suspects so that we could be held to account. This did not happen. And in the meantime, as Ivo Rajkovic was also the director and the monitor - I think this was in December - he managed to get Rajkovic transferred to Croatia because his entire family was in Croatia, but his wife is a citizen of Croatia from Dubrovnik, I think, so that his children, his wife, and his brothers were there and he got out. I asked the wife what she was doing, what we could do. And then she said that Mr. Cuskic had said, "It would be best for you to leave Travnik."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did there come a time -- to move on, did there come a time when you were finally released? And can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to when this happened.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I wasn't officially released. But it happened in the following way: When everything had been settled between the International Red Cross and UNPROFOR, in order to evacuate us from Travnik, and when on the 18th of January, 1994 we were supposed to leave, someone put up resistance to this. That's what Mary Jo said. And this had to do with the military presidency in Travnik and the command of the 3rd Corps in Zenica. The Travnik authorities wouldn't allow it, and the military authorities wouldn't allow it in Zenica, and Mrs. Mary Jo wasn't able to solve this, so that on the 18th, when these all-terrain vehicles, et cetera, arrived to transfer us, this release didn't take place. I remained in the barracks for another ten days, and one evening - I think it was on the 30th in the afternoon - on the 31st of January, through Dr. Begzad I asked to be seen by Cuskic to see what should be done now. Cuskic told me that there was really nothing more he could tell me other than what he had already told me, so then I said that I would leave the barracks alone. And if someone had to eliminate them, they should do so because it wasn't appropriate for me to be kept in such a position any more. When Mr. Begzad returned, the doctor, he told me what I have already said that, Cuskic had no more business with me. I then gathered my possessions, went to the reception area. No one stopped me. No one asked me why I didn't have an escort with me. And I went home. And that is how I left the barracks in Travnik. That is how I was released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Fisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. I'm going to give the floor to the Defence, who are going to ask you several questions. But before that, I have several questions myself in order to -- for you to clarify the answers that you have given to the Prosecution. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You spoke about the person who was decapitated, Mr. Dragan Popovic. Who was that person? What was his official position? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: This person was a native of Travnik. He had a degree in economics. He worked in the Sebesic company. He was a financial expert. And according to the assignment of citizens to duties during the imminent threat of war, according to the old system, before the elections he was a member of the reserve police of the municipality of Travnik. He remained on the strength of the reserve police up to the year 1993, the beginning of 1993. Then he was returned to his previous position, to the company where he became financial director, and that was his official position at the moment when he was arrested. His wife is my neighbour, also an economist. She worked in the forestry company as an employee of the transport department. They were just normal citizens of Travnik. So I am speaking about the person who was a native of Travnik, who was born and bred in Travnik. And as I have already said, he came from a mixed marriage. His father was a Serb of the Orthodox religion, and his mother was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. When you were taken to the execution site, although you were detained together with him, why was he chosen of all of you? Why were others not chosen to be executed? So what made him to be chosen that day?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I don't have a precise answer to your question. I don't know why. I don't know why I was detained, to this very day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Another question: You have told us that at the execution site there were about 50 Mujahedins or about 50 persons, and you also told us that there was a vehicle there. The 50 people who were there, you saw them. According to you, was there somebody who was in command of these persons or were there just independent agents, so to speak? Was there a hierarchical structure according to which one of them was in command?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I didn't recognise any such structure. And if I had been told who to address, I would have done that. But nobody told us that. We were just numbers. What I saw was a ritual that was led by an Arab person. Whether he was in command or not, I don't know. I must tell you that there were two people from Travnik, Nektib [phoen], a foreign citizen, who had been in Travnik from before the war. He was a student at the Sarajevo university; and an interpreter, Huso Delic, who was at that time the Secretary of the Interior of Travnik Municipality. These persons could enter freely this camp. The latter was the official interpreter, and the former person was the person of trust who was always with them. I believe that we were transported in his vehicle, the Niva vehicle. And I also know for sure that he was one of those who were there on Friday, when Kazimir was allowed to return to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You've also told us that there was a vehicle which was close to the execution site. You have marked the position of that vehicle on the photo. Can you confirm that there was a vehicle and whose vehicle that was?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the type of the vehicle. It was an all-terrain vehicle, darkened windows. It was metallic grey. I used to see that vehicle in Travnik, and it belonged to the MOS. Who was in the vehicle, I wouldn't be able to tell you because I didn't see. I didn't look too hard, but I recognised the vehicle because I recognised it from Travnik. I had seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I would like to thank you for this clarification. And my last question to you, arising from your answer: You have told us that Mr. Fikret Cuskic heard what you had said, and according to you he was the commander of the 25th unit. He should have called President Izetbegovic and he arrived in the barracks. According to you, the arrival of Mr. Izetbegovic, is it directly connected to what you said to Mr. Cuskic?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat and I'll clarify what I've said. When we went to Mr. Cuskic, he listened to us very carefully, very patiently. But he reacted very nervously and he said, "I can no longer be a soldier in this area if things continue like this. And I'm going to ask Mr. Izetbegovic to deal with this." That's what he told us. After that, Mr. Izetbegovic did visit Travnik and Bugojno. Whether there was any discussion on those issues at that meeting or not, I don't know. However, I noticed that after that, Mektauf could not longer enter the compound of the barracks. The gate was closed to him, and his presence was no longer seen in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm going to give the floor to the Defence for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Fisic. I am Edina Residovic. I represent General Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will mostly stay within the context of the questions put by the Prosecution, but in order to seek some clarification I am also going to ask Mr. Fisic to answer a few questions about the general situation in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, before the war, you were a prominent person in Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am a bit far from the microphone, so I'll move closer. You discharged various duties. You were the general manager of Borac Travnik for the longest time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to your duties in the business life, you were also a very active in the social and political life and you discharged various duties in the League of Communists and the Socialist Alliance, but this was always a voluntary position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1981, you were elected as president of the executive committee of the municipality, that is, of the municipal government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1990, there were the first so-called multiparty elections, and in those elections the ethnic party won the elections; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is true of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Travnik, the winners were the SDA and the HDZ and to a lesser extent the SDS, and they formed the government composed of ethnically based parties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how the government was composed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that time, you never opted for any of these parties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already told us that at the beginning of the war you were the general manager of one of the companies within the Borac company which engaged in printing and trade in printed matters. And you stayed in that position up to mid-1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
