utterances.text: Due to the war and everything else that you have mentioned in your testimony, very quickly there were some divisions in the government, the government which was composed of the ethnically based parties. The HDZ left government and formed its own HVO government.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: It would be more precise to say that the president of the presidency at that time, of the Travnik municipality, Mr. Tamburic, realised that the conflicts and that discords could no longer persist. And conclusion was issued at that session, which consisted of eight items. He looked for some new people who could help to overcome the prevailing situation, and that was the reason why I joined the HVO structure -- but the civilian structure, mind you. We wanted to create a single government. I'm talking about my role. I wouldn't go any further. We managed at the end of the day to form a government that nobody respected. And as soon as it was formed, new conflicts started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would have been my next question. So your efforts to form a single government timely fell through and there were no results. That was fruitless. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The attempts to form a single government were the result of the bad relationship between the War Presidency and the representatives of the HDZ at the end of April 1993, when it was ordered to the HVO authorities to leave the building of the municipality up to -- in which up to then it had its headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to a different topic. You participated in a certain way in the attempt to form a single government, so you will know that the War Presidency of the municipality, as well as the civilian HVO government, were actually civilian branches of authorities in Travnik municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a matter of time, throughout the war in Travnik there was never military government, so to speak. Throughout this time, the military formations were separate from the civilian government.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: The police forces were also separate from the civic forces. The police was under the command of somebody else rather than of the civilian government in Travnik. I mean the presidency and the civilian sector of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, let's clarify this. The civilian police had its line of command and its superior body was the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that true?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: At that time, there were some invisible forces that were in command, and I cannot tell you who they were. In any case, it was not the situation that arose from the security situation in Travnik. We wanted to deal with the matter, but they did not respect what they said -- what we said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a citizen of Travnik and a participant in the organs of power, can you please confirm before this Trial Chamber that the overall situation in Travnik after the beginning of the war was very complex and was compounded by the refugees who flocked into Travnik in great numbers.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I believe that the situation in Travnik was compounded by the failure of agreement amongst the international forces - I'm referring to the Vance-Owen Plan and Stoltenberg Plan - and I believe that this created lot more tension in Travnik than refugees. It is true that there were refugees there and that -- and that people left Travnik in rather unpleasant circumstances. And what I'm saying is that only people who did not have anywhere else to go remained in Travnik. But in any case, there was a significant number of refugees. They were poor, and there were many refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is it also true that in Travnik at that time new organs of power were being formed to represent those refugees -- the Banja Luka district, the Travnik district -- so all of a sudden in Travnik there were several bodies of government, several authorities which tried to exert influence on the population who resided in Travnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: This wouldn't be correct. The process of forming of War Presidencies and other bodies that represented other areas and other people who resided in Travnik, this existed, but after the conflict between Croats and Muslims. This did not exist before the 4th of June. These organs were created after the 4th of June, after the conflict Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. between the Croats and Muslims, which happened on the 4th of June or sometime between the 4th and the 6th of June, in any case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am also not sure about the dates, but we are talking about the year 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: In 1993, yes, these bodies did exist. After the 4th of June, there was a conflict, and these bodies were established in Travnik to represent other people who had fled from different areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the Prosecutor's question, you replied that in the course of 1992, in the summer of 1992 you started noticing foreigners in the town of Travnik. These people arrived in Travnik via third countries, and you said that they were Arabs.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I think I was right when I said that they were Arabs. I believe that their origins were Arabic. I don't know whether they were from Algiers or from Tunis. Hamza, for example, was an Arab. He was an Arabic person. And he was well known in Travnik. He was well known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was not in Travnik; you were. But I wanted to ask you whether it is correct that the commander of these Arabs was a person known as Hamza.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes. He tried to introduce a new order in Travnik. He, for example, wouldn't allow coffee bars to serve alcoholic drinks. He, also, because of that, came in clash with the people from Krajina. He tried to instil fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let's try with first things first. From the very beginning they were something that caused anxiety and then fear amongst both Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I believe that quite a lot of the Muslim population found them undesirable. They didn't try to fight them, but they found them undesirable. And very soon it was realised that these people would be a peril for everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ribo Haso was also one of those who opposed their influence in the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I know Haso Ribo, but I would not hesitate to say that I don't know to what extent he opposed. If he had, then he was absolutely powerless. This is just my speculation. He -- they relied on their priests, on their religious officials, who laid the ground for their actions. They said that they did not belong to any units and they could do whatever they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You seem to be reading my mind. You have already answered my next question. It was obvious that these people rallied around various Muslim humanitarian and religious organisations and individual, Merhamet and over others, and that they found support in those organisations and people.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: In Travnik, I believe that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, it was obvious that these people had a lot of money and that this fact also had a bearing on the local population which started rallying around them and imitating them.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I believe that their relationship was symbiotic, that there was a symbiotic relationship with these foreigners who had political goals who could incorporate quite nicely into the structure of the people that found this favourable. Some people found material interest, and some people, on the other hand, were convinced that this is the right road for the Bosniak Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the commander, Fikret Cuskic, was the commander of the 27th Krajina Brigade. If I were to put to you that it was the 17th Krajina Brigade at the time, could you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I can accept that. It was the 17th, not the 27th. I correct myself -- I stand corrected on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were talking about your attempt to form a joint government, one of those people who offered certain positions to you and did it even after the conflict in June, he offered you to join the local administration, that was Dr. Genjac, at the time president of the local SDA, the ethnically-based party of the Muslim people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the conflict in Travnik, you remained in Travnik together with your family. You're still there. However, for a few days you didn't go to work. And when you eventually returned to work, you realised that the local authorities had replaced the management board of your company. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Let me be more precise. I stayed with my family in Travnik, not with my entire family. My two children on that day, on that unfortunate day when the conflict happened -- my wife's family lives about 3 to 5 kilometres away from Travnik. There was no school. My children went with my in-laws. They abandoned their house. They went barefoot because they had been walking around the house. So I stayed in Travnik with my wife, my sister as well, and her son stayed up there in the same manner. So this is a more precise answer as to the composition of my family in Travnik. As for Mr. Genjac, it is true that he offered us to penetrate - that's his expression - into the organs of power. We couldn't accept that because we were not elected by -- on behalf of the HDZ. We would have been intruders. We wanted to have a legitimate status. And it was up to them to run the politics as they thought it was appropriate and protect the interests of the citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, when you returned to your company where you were the general manager, you realised that a new management board had been established. You didn't want to work with them, and that's why you resigned and you abandoned the position of the general manager.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. For a few days I stayed at home. Some people visited me, my friends. Muslims visited me, and they were of the opinion that I shouldn't leave the house because there were some people who could do me harm. A few days later I went to my company. I met with the president of the supervisory board, and we saw that our company, just like the others, had sustained some damage. Nothing major actually happened, but there was some damage. And then I realised that the economy department of Travnik municipality appointed Dalo Muhar [phoen] and Halilovic Mersad. One of them was in charge of the marketing and the other was in charge of municipal affairs -- they did that without having consulted me first. According to the then-prevailing instructions on the operations of companies in war conditions, I should have been consulted. I took that as a sign of mistrust, and I started the procedure to be removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You replaced certain persons in Travnik at the time. Huso Delic, whom you mentioned, was the chief of the Travnik MUP. You mentioned these persons --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: Not replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was able to enter the Orasac camp, and he acted as an interpreter for the Mujahedin and other people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: That's what I know about for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, the president of the civilian authorities of the War Presidency was Mehmet Curcic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the Presiding Judge, you said that you -- or rather, this is what you said earlier on. You said you had been taken away in a Lada Niva vehicle. And in response to a question from the Presiding Judge, you recognised that this was a vehicle that belonged to Mektauf; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mektauf was an Arab who had been living in Travnik, and he cooperated with these Arabs and was involved in various duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I think that everyone from Travnik would confirm that, and I will too, so yes, he was in Travnik. Up until the war, he was someone who ran a discotheque, and he lived probably happily with his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was another Arab who lived in Travnik before the war. His name was Tafija and he was a dentist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he lives in Travnik to this day. He's married to a woman from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when you were taken to Orasac, you found out from your wife and later on from the wife of the late Popovic too, that when attempting to obtain information about you and to obtain your release, they went both to Mektauf and Tafija, as they thought that they were persons who had influence with these foreigners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: My wife and my sister didn't go to see them. My sister went to the Travnik mufti. She thought he had a certain influence. She knew him from before. He wouldn't see her and he refused to help her. Mektauf is a friend of Popovic Kazimir. He worked as an engineer for him. He carried out construction work on his discotheque, and they knew each other. But Ljilja Popovic was a friend of my wife and of Tafija. She went to see Tafija. So my family didn't go so see Tafija and Mektauf. They went to Nusret Efendija and to see other religious people who might have had some influence and might have been able to obtain our release.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your wife and Mrs. Popovic, as far as I've understood from your answers, you spoke to them later and in fact contacted a number of persons. They contacted Mr. Genjac, the president of the SDA, and Huso Delic, the chief of the civilian police. And now you have just explained something about Mektauf. And they contacted the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Cuskic. But is it correct to say that they told you, what Commander Cuskic and Commander Alagic said was they would do all they could to get your release?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I would like to confirm that the late Mr. Alagic and Mr. Cuskic did all they could to obtain our release. That is the impression I'm under. As to what else they did in the course of the war, I wouldn't like to say. But as far as we are concerned -- as far as I am concerned, as far as my wife and sister are concerned -- they were very fair and we were treated correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A while ago you said that when you were arrested, Fikret Cuskic was the commander of the 17th Krajina Brigade. And at the time, Mehmet Alagic was the commander of the operative group of Bosnian Krajina in the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I think that that was the structure at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were released on the 6th of November.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I was forcibly removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You got to the barracks from Orasac on the 6th of November though; is that isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until you left the barracks and went home, you saw Commander Cuskic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to repeat everything that you have said that you spoke to him about, but would it be correct to say that at the time you did not meet Commander Alagic, because he had gone to Zenica where he took over the duties as commander of the 3rd Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I didn't meet the late Alagic there. He was still in Travnik. And rumour had it that he would be transferred to Zenica. So no, I didn't establish contact of any kind with Mr. Alagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Commander Cuskic replaced Commander Alagic after he went to Zenica and took over the duties of 3rd Corps command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: That would be in the month of December, I think. So yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That information is contained in the documents.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that is how the events unfolded.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does the Defence team for Mr. Kubura have any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Charged with any incidents that this witness has testified about, there are no questions for this witness on behalf of Mr. Kubura. I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. Is there any re-examination for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President, Your Honours. Re-examined by Mr. Withopf:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fisic, these soldiers whom you have seen at the Orasac camp, were they all Mujahedin, meaning foreign soldiers, or did you also -- did you also see local --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise, but I didn't ask any questions about Orasac, so there are no grounds for re-examining the witness with regard to issues that weren't touched upon by the Defence in the course of its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Defence says that as these questions weren't put to the witness, you are now asking the witness to provide clarifications. Normally you should ask for clarifications about questions asked by the Defence, but as the Defence didn't ask any questions about this group of 50 persons, this is not appropriate. It's something you should have asked before. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Trial Chamber actually asked such a question, and I wish to clarify the answer the witness has given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll withdraw to deliberate for a few minutes to see whether we may allow you to ask this question. --- Break taken at 12.10 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has deliberated in order to determine whether the Prosecution could ask the witness to clarify what the composition of the group of 50 persons was. After having heard the objection raised by the Defence -- the Trial Chamber has taken note of the objection raised by the Defence. As far as the Prosecution's request is concerned and the Defence's position, on the basis of Rule 89, the Trial Chamber will ask the witness this question; although, the answers that he has already provided make the issue clear. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in order to be quite clear, Witness, I'm going to put a question to you along the lines of what has already been asked of you. The 50 people that were there, were they all Mujahedin or were there others who were there too, people who weren't Mujahedin? It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: I couldn't identify the Mujahedin and others, but I can say that most of the soldiers were members of the El Mujahed unit, and they were mostly local people. So they were part of the El Mujahed unit, so they were most likely Mujahedin themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that most of them were part of the El Mujahed unit, but you have added that there were some local people, people from the area too. There were some local Muslims.

utterances.speaker: IVO FISIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Bosnian Muslims from various areas. But they were part of that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we have heard your answer. The Prosecution may continue, but please ensure that your questions relate to the questions put to the witness in the course of the Defence's cross-examination. If necessary, the Trial Chamber can also ask some questions to obtain clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. The Prosecution has no further questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Witness, you have answered the questions put to you by the Prosecution and the Defence for one of the accused. You have also answered questions put to you by the Judges. Thank you for having testified. At one point in time you said that - and you were addressing the Trial Chamber - you said that you wanted your medical condition to be checked here in The Hague, and it appeared that you said that you were still suffering from the consequences of your injuries. So this question which you have put to the Trial Chamber, I must have to say that according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence the Trial Chamber doesn't have any power. In this situation, it's not possible; in other situations, it might be possible. But the Rules of Procedure are such that the Trial Chamber cannot grant your request, we cannot grant your request for a medical checkup. However, there is the Victims and Witnesses Unit here, and when you are escorted out of the courtroom, the Victims and Witnesses Unit will take charge of you and you can ask them this question. And then on the basis of the answer you get -- regardless of the answer you get, you should contact someone in your country to see what the various procedures might be in order to have your request satisfied there. But this Trial Chamber cannot grant the very precise request you have made. Having said that, thank you for your testimony. We wish you a good trip home. And I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I hope that I have helped justice to be done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We don't have any witnesses scheduled. Yesterday I pointed out that we would resume our hearings on Tuesday morning, since we'll be sitting in the morning next week. Monday is a holiday, so we will resume on Tuesday morning. The CD-ROM question is one that we still have to deal with, but this matter will be resolved as soon as possible. The Trial Chamber still has to hand down a number of decisions which are still pending. We will do so rapidly, since they are in the process of being completed. In addition, at the beginning of next week -- we have not yet received this letter from the European Union. We're waiting to receive it, to read it. It has been promised to us. But perhaps you will have other information for us on Tuesday when we resume with our hearing. If there are no more issues to be raised, in that case we will adjourn, and I will see everyone next week on Tuesday at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 3rd day of February, 2004 at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.24 p.m.,
